analysis.one_liner: Eliminates federal tax on long-term investment gains for assets bought or sold in 2009–2010.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor; it sat in the Ways and Means Committee until the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have let investors pay no federal income tax on profits from selling stocks, real estate, or other assets they held for more than a year, as long as the asset was bought or sold between January 1, 2009 and December 31, 2010 — a window covering the depths of the financial crisis, when many long-held assets were sold at depressed prices. Because the window was retroactive to 2009, it would have wiped out tax bills for sales that had already happened. The bill was introduced by Rep. Parker Griffith in March 2009, drew no cosponsors, and was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up; it died there when the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors with taxable profits on assets sold or bought during 2009–2010 would have paid no federal tax on those long-term gains. The largest benefits would have gone to households with the biggest investment portfolios — including funds, hedge funds, and wealthy individuals selling appreciated stock, real estate, or business assets during the crisis — since capital gains are concentrated among high-income taxpayers.

how_it_helps.text: It would have excluded from taxable income any gain from the sale of a capital asset held more than one year, so long as the asset was bought or sold between January 1, 2009 and December 31, 2010.
The exclusion applied retroactively to tax years ending after December 31, 2008, covering sales that had already taken place when the bill was introduced.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers collectively, through either a larger deficit or spending cuts elsewhere, since the bill contained no revenue offsets for the trillions in capital gains realized nationally during the window.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers generally, via lost revenue

drawbacks.text: The bill contained no revenue offsets, so a two-year exemption for investment gains would have increased the federal deficit or required cuts elsewhere to pay for it.

Because it applied to assets 'acquired or disposed of' during 2009–2010, taxpayers could have sold long-held assets at depressed crisis-era prices and excluded even large gains on assets held for years before the window opened, making the benefit far broader than a stimulus measure for new 2009–2010 investment.

Capital gains are disproportionately earned by high-income households, so the exclusion would have concentrated its benefits among those with the largest investment holdings and done little for working people whose income comes from wages.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits would have gone overwhelmingly to households with large investment gains — including gains on assets sold during the financial crisis — while the cost would have been spread across all federal taxpayers through a larger deficit, or borne through program cuts had an offset been required. Weighed honestly, a tax break of this size with no revenue offset and no safeguard against claiming it on recent loss-recovery gains is poorly designed as public policy; as a stimulus measure its effect would also have been weak, since it rewarded already-completed sales rather than encouraging new investment. The bill never advanced far enough for these tradeoffs to be debated.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or sent it to the full House before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on March 12, 2009 and referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
No further action was ever taken: the record shows no hearings, no committee vote, no floor action, and no vote in either chamber.
The bill attracted no cosponsors at any point during the two-year Congress.
The bill died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, without ever being reported out of committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal revenue was preserved, since a two-year exemption on long-term capital gains — worth most to investors with the largest gains — never became law. No other group gained; the bill simply expired unnoticed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal taxpayers, by avoiding the cost of the exemption

for.name: Rep. Parker Griffith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 12, 2009, proposing a two-year exclusion of long-term capital gains from taxable income.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never attracted a cosponsor from either party and never reached a vote, so no partisan split on the substance was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Investors and holders of appreciated assets
industries.note: A two-year federal tax exemption on long-term investment gains — including sales already made during the financial crisis — would have eliminated capital gains tax for this group for 2009–2010 transactions.

Suspending capital gains tax for two years would have encouraged investors to buy and sell assets within the window, generating transaction activity, though the effect is secondary since the bill was never enacted.
